claims.text: Cold rolling by approximately 80% followed by annealing at about 750 °C for 20 minutes will improve the room-temperature ductility of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo without a major loss of yield strength.
As-cast equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered single-phase BCC solid solution.
The as-cast alloy has approximately 100 μm equiaxed grains.
The as-cast alloy has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
Approximately 80% cold rolling induces substantial work hardening and crystallographic orientation in NbZrTiHfMo.
Cold rolling produces dislocation tangles or walls, low- and medium-angle boundaries, strong texture, and elongated grains.
Annealing the cold-rolled alloy near 750 °C for 20 minutes produces partial recrystallization and recovery.
Partial recrystallization and recovery refine the microstructure and reduce excessive impediments to dislocation slip.
Cold rolling increases strength through work hardening and grain elongation but decreases ductility.
Intermediate-temperature annealing eases dislocation motion by reducing excessive dislocation density and inhomogeneous grain-boundary structures.
Retaining part of the cold-worked microstructure after annealing preserves sufficient barriers to maintain high yield strength.
High Mo content increases electronegativity differences and hinders plasticity in equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
The recovery and partial-recrystallization balance can counteract the adverse effect of high Mo content on plasticity.
The treated alloy will retain compressive yield strength within approximately 10–15% of 1719 MPa.
The treated alloy will exhibit at least about a 50% increase in room-temperature plastic strain relative to the as-cast alloy.
The beneficial processing window is approximately 700–800 °C with a short annealing duration around 20 minutes.
Annealing at substantially higher temperatures or for longer times could cause full recrystallization and erode strength.
Less aggressive thermomechanical treatments may leave the alloy with insufficient plasticity.
The strength–ductility response is sensitive to small changes in annealing temperature and duration.
